title: A useless slaughter (1917)
hookLine: Benedict XV calls the Great War a useless slaughter and proposes peace

lines: A LETTER TO THE NATIONS AT WAR.
cards: Across Europe, men are living in trenches, and whole villages have been emptied. From the Vatican, a letter goes out, addressed to the leaders of the nations at war.
Catholic soldiers fight on both sides, praying to the same God in the same Mass, on opposite sides of the wire. The letter is from Pope Benedict XV. It doesn't bless a side.
It names the war for what he thinks it is.

teach.b: First, the phrase. Benedict asked whether the civilized world must become a field of death, and he called the war a useless slaughter. Not glorious, not holy.
Second, the plan. He didn't stop at grief.

He proposed terms: that the moral force of right should take the place of the force of arms, that nations reduce their weapons together, that disputes go to arbitration instead of battle, that the seas be free, and that occupied lands be given back.
Governments on both sides turned it down or ignored it, and some accused him of secretly favoring the enemy. The war went on. Fourth, the other work.
While the plan failed, the Vatican did what it could beside it: helping find missing soldiers, passing news between prisoners and their families, and sending relief to the hungry.
In the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." Notice that the line doesn't promise peacemakers success.
Benedict XV didn't get his peace. What he left was a plan on paper and a name for the war: useless slaughter, from a pope who would not call it glorious.

how: Catholics pray for peace and for those at war in the prayers of the faithful at Mass, and later popes have also appealed for peace; some parishes remember Benedict XV's peace note when they mark the anniversary of the First World War.

games.q: you're the pope. Catholics are fighting on both sides of a great war. what do you do?
o: support the side with more Catholics.
call it a useless slaughter and propose terms for peace.
games.why: he wrote to the warring nations with a plan. both sides rejected it, and the war went on.

practice: Bring to mind people in uniform right now, on any side of any conflict: someone young on watch at night, someone wounded, someone home who can't sleep, a family waiting by a phone.
If you pray, hold them before God without asking which side they're on; if not, hold them in your attention and wish them safety and a way home.

wordCard.voice: Inutile strage. Italian for useless slaughter, the phrase remembered from Pope Benedict XV's letter calling the Great War useless and proposing terms for peace.

orig.note: Italian: useless slaughter, the phrase from Benedict XV's peace note remembered in Italian.

carryVoice: Your line: useless slaughter. A pope who would not bless a side. See you tomorrow.
